cacheInvalidation.title: Cache updates and invalidation
cacheInvalidation.heading: Cache updates and invalidation
cacheInvalidation.lead: Applications use caches to reduce repeated database reads, but a cached copy can become stale after the database changes. This page uses cache-aside: readers fill on demand, and writers commit the database before deleting the cached entry. Concurrency and failures can still produce stale data.
cacheInvalidation.footer: This example uses an application-managed shared cache and reads from the primary database. Actual consistency depends on storage, concurrency control, and failure recovery. See also webhook event notifications.
cacheInvalidation.overview:
flowchart LR
    R[Reader instance] -->|Look up| C[(Cache)]
    R -.->|Read on miss| D[(Primary database)]
    R -.->|Fill on miss| C
    W[Writer instance] -->|Commit new value first| D
    W -->|Delete key after commit| C
cacheInvalidation.overviewNote: Reader and writer instances represent application requests that can run concurrently. Dashed arrows occur only on a cache miss; a window exists between the database write and cache deletion.
cacheInvalidation.supplement:
Three common cache update approaches

ApproachWhat happens after a writeConsiderations
Invalidate on writeCommit to the database, then delete affected cache entries; the next read reloads them.Relatively direct, but failed deletion, concurrent refill, or replica lag can still produce stale values.
Update on writeCoordinate a cache update with the data-store write, for example with write-through caching.Can reduce cold misses, but cross-system failure and concurrent writes still need coordination; strong consistency is not automatic.
Rely on expirationDo not actively propagate every update; reload after the cache entry expires.Simple but can serve stale data for a long time. Refill timing and sliding expiration affect the actual duration.

Approaches can be combined. First decide how much staleness the business can tolerate, then choose mechanisms and verify their actual guarantees.

Concurrency and failure boundaries

  • Race window: An old read can fill the cache after a write and deletion. Durable version fences, atomic conditional fills, or coordination covering every access path are possible designs; comparing a version only while the cache key exists cannot stop an old value recreating a deleted key.
  • Reliable invalidation: Deletion can fail after commit. A transactional outbox with reliable delivery, change-data capture, retries, and alerts can compensate, but delays, duplicates, and reordered messages still need handling.
  • Expiration: A fixed TTL limits the lifetime of a particular cache write. Slow reads filling later, repeated writes, or sliding expiration can extend inconsistency measured from a database update. TTL alone is not an unconditional strong-consistency guarantee.
  • Read source and cache scope: Replica lag, multiple local cache layers, and other services writing the database can bypass this invalidation path. Cover all affected keys and writers.
  • Load and failure: A hot key expiring can cause many simultaneous database reads. Request coalescing or appropriate rate limits can help. Plan database capacity for cache failures; critical reads requiring strong consistency need a data path that provides the required guarantee.

References: Microsoft Cache-Aside pattern · Redis cache-aside

paymentIdempotency.title: Payment idempotency: safely retrying a payment
paymentIdempotency.heading: Payment idempotency: safely retrying a payment
paymentIdempotency.lead: After a payment request times out, a merchant may not know whether the payment provider executed it. An idempotency key lets an endpoint that supports the feature recognize repeated requests for the same operation and reduce duplicate-charge risk. The merchant still needs to handle unknown outcomes, key expiry, and reconciliation.
paymentIdempotency.footer: This example assumes the payment provider supports idempotency keys and the first payment succeeds but its response is lost. Continue with webhook event notifications and 3D Secure authentication.
paymentIdempotency.overviewTitle: Overview: retrying with the same key
paymentIdempotency.overview:
flowchart LR
    U[User] -->|Confirm payment| M[Merchant service]
    M -->|Payment request and key K| P[Payment provider]
    P -->|Save operation state| D[(Idempotency records)]
    P -.->|Lost response causes timeout| M
    M -.->|Retry same request and K under policy| P
    P -->|Look up recorded result| D
    P -->|Return payment result| M
paymentIdempotency.overviewNote: Solid arrows show the normal request, record, and result; dashed arrows show the conditional path when the response is lost. Duplicate request handling depends on the provider’s API.
paymentIdempotency.supplement:
Which requests use the same key

SituationKey and parametersWhat to check
Retry the same operation after a timeoutReuse the original key and parameters within the provider’s permitted window.Check endpoint support and retry rules; a timeout does not mean failure.
Same key with a different amount or other parametersDo not reuse it; the provider may reject mismatched requests.A parameter change may indicate another operation. First check the original payment status.
New payment operation or refundUse a new operation identifier and key; reuse that key when retrying the same new operation.First confirm the new operation is appropriate, rather than treating an unknown outcome as failure.

An idempotency key identifies one business operation; it is not a general replacement for an order ID. One order can have multiple independent operations.

Implementation boundaries

  • Scope and expiry: Confirm endpoint support, key scope, retention, and error response rules. An expired key may no longer deduplicate; behavior differs among providers.
  • Concurrency and persistence: Before the first request, durably save the operation and key. Coordinate concurrent merchant instances with a uniqueness constraint or equivalent; the provider also needs atomic duplicate detection. Handle in-progress, conflict, and parameter mismatch responses under its API rules.
  • Cross-system uncertainty: Local deduplication does not make downstream funds operations atomic with local records. Keep the original payment identifier, query status, process trusted notifications, and reconcile; investigate manually when needed.
  • Business status: Interpret an API response using the actual payment status. A request being accepted does not itself mean final settlement. Payments, captures, and refunds each have separate operations and states.
  • Security and retries: Generate sufficiently unique random keys without sensitive information. Use bounded backoff and monitoring, and follow provider rules for retryable errors and timing.

References: Stripe idempotent requests · PayPal API requests

webhook.title: Webhook event notifications
webhook.heading: Webhook event notifications
webhook.lead: When an event occurs in one service, a webhook lets the event provider send an HTTP notification to an address configured by the receiver. The receiver verifies and stores the event, then processes it asynchronously. Delivery success does not mean business processing succeeded, and retry and message formats depend on the provider.
webhook.footer: This example uses HTTPS POST and shared-secret signatures; consult the event provider for its verification and redelivery rules. Continue with payment idempotency and 3D Secure.
webhook.overviewTitle: Overview: delivering and processing an event
webhook.overview:
flowchart LR
    P[Event provider] -->|POST event and signature| E[Receiver endpoint]
    E -->|Verify and save event| Q[(Durable storage)]
    E -->|Success response| P
    W[Background worker] -->|Read and update state| Q
    P -.->|Automatic retry or manual redelivery| E
webhook.overviewNote: Solid arrows show durable receipt and background processing. The dashed path applies after delivery failure when the provider supports automatic retry or the integrator requests redelivery.
webhook.supplement:
Delivery, receipt, and processing are different states

StateResponsibilityRecovery
HTTP deliveryThe provider sends a notification and the receiver responds.Retry automatically, redeliver manually, or reconcile as supported; not every provider retries automatically.
Durable receiptThe endpoint verifies the message and persists the event and pending status.Do not acknowledge success when storage fails; if the response is lost after saving, redelivery may create a duplicate.
Business processingThe receiver’s background worker applies the operation and records its outcome.The receiver retries, alerts, or recovers manually; HTTP success does not guarantee this step succeeded.

The provider defines how event identifiers can be used for deduplication. If different events can trigger the same business operation, protect side effects using a business identifier too.

Integration boundaries

  • Verify origin and integrity: Use HTTPS, verify signatures as the provider specifies, and protect secrets. When signed timestamps are supported, check their permitted time window. Signature verification does not replace business authorization or field validation.
  • Duplicates and concurrency: Deduplicate atomically using the provider’s event identifier and appropriate scope. Design durable pending records and idempotent business processing together to avoid loss or duplication during concurrency and crashes.
  • Ordering and gaps: Do not assume delivery order matches event order. Apply business version or state-transition rules to old events; query the provider API for current state and reconcile when needed.
  • Operations and recovery: Limit request sizes, keep safe logs, and monitor delivery and processing failures. Do not expose signing secrets or sensitive data in logs. Define redelivery, exhausted retry, and manual recovery procedures.

References: GitHub webhook best practices · Handling failed GitHub deliveries

oidcLogin.title: OpenID Connect login
oidcLogin.heading: OpenID Connect login
oidcLogin.lead: OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds authentication to the OAuth 2.0 authorization flow. After an identity provider authenticates the user, the application validates the identity in an ID token and creates its own login session. This example uses a server-side application with PKCE.
oidcLogin.footer: This page illustrates a common OIDC authorization code login. Continue with OAuth 2.0 and PKCE, single sign-on and logout, and session cookies.
oidcLogin.overviewTitle: Overview: how the application confirms the user’s identity
oidcLogin.overview:
flowchart LR
    U[User] -->|Choose login| B[Browser]
    B -->|Visit and callback| C[Application]
    B -->|Authenticate user| I[Identity provider]
    C -->|Code and verifier| I
    I -->|ID token and access token| C
    C -->|Create application session| B
oidcLogin.overviewNote: The browser carries redirects; the application gets and validates identity information from the token endpoint, then creates its own session.
oidcLogin.supplement:
What the two tokens do

TokenRecipient and purposeKey boundary
ID tokenSent to the application to convey the provider’s authentication result and user identifier.The application validates the signature and claims; it is not an access token for APIs.
Access tokenThe client presents it to a protected resource or the UserInfo endpoint.The resource server checks the token and permissions; it is not itself proof of login to the application.

For additional user information, the application can call UserInfo when authorized. Its returned sub must match the validated ID token’s sub before the information is used.

Authentication and session boundaries

  • OIDC and OAuth: OAuth primarily addresses authorization; OIDC adds authentication using the openid scope and ID token.
  • Trusted configuration: Obtain configuration and keys from a trusted issuer; check the expected issuer, audience, algorithm, token validity and the nonce sent in this example.
  • Identity: Identify a user by the combination of iss and sub. Email and other profile information can change and are not stable identifiers across providers.
  • Logout scope: Ending the application session does not necessarily end the provider’s or other applications’ sessions. Logout propagation depends on their support and configuration.

References: OpenID Connect Core · OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice

oauthPkce.title: OAuth 2.0 authorization code and PKCE
oauthPkce.heading: OAuth 2.0 authorization code and PKCE
oauthPkce.lead: When a user wants an application to access their resources at another service, OAuth 2.0 lets the application obtain an access token from an authorization server. This example uses a server-side client and a browser to show the authorization code flow and how Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) binds the code to the request.
oauthPkce.footer: This example uses a server-side client and S256; endpoints and permissions depend on the provider. Continue with OIDC single sign-on and access and refresh tokens.
oauthPkce.overviewTitle: Overview: from user authorization to resource access
oauthPkce.overview:
flowchart LR
    U[User] -->|Operates| B[Browser]
    B -->|Start and callback| C[Client application]
    B -->|Login and consent| A[Authorization server]
    C -->|Code and verifier| A
    A -->|Access token| C
    C -->|Token and resource request| R[Resource server]
    R -->|Protected resource| C
oauthPkce.overviewNote: The browser carries the authorization request and callback; the client exchanges the code at the token endpoint and uses the access token to request resources.
oauthPkce.supplement:
How PKCE binds the code

For each request, the client generates a random code_verifier and calculates code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(ASCII(code_verifier))) without padding. The authorization request sends only the challenge; the verifier is sent over HTTPS during exchange. The server recalculates and compares the challenge, preventing someone who intercepts only the code from redeeming it.

PKCE does not protect an access token that has already leaked or replace secure verifier storage, callback validation, or client protection.

Authorization and authentication boundaries

  • Scope: scope describes requested access; the authorization server determines what is granted and the resource server must still check permissions.
  • Client type: Public clients cannot reliably keep a client secret and must use PKCE. PKCE is also recommended for confidential clients, which still authenticate as required.
  • Callback protection: This example binds state to the user session to correlate the callback and prevent cross-site request forgery; the authorization server should strictly match registered redirect URIs.
  • Authentication: OAuth is an authorization framework; an access token should not itself be treated as proof of login to the client. For login, use OIDC and validate the ID token.

References: RFC 6749 · RFC 7636 · RFC 9700

sessionCookie.lead: The server stores login state and sends an opaque session identifier in Set-Cookie. The browser sends the cookie on matching requests, allowing the server to find the session.
sessionCookie.overview:
flowchart LR
 B[Browser] -->|Credentials| S[Server]
 S -->|Save session| D[(Session store)]
 S -->|Set-Cookie| B
 B -->|Later request with cookie| S
 S -->|Look up session| D
 S -->|Response| B
sessionCookie.overviewNote: The cookie carries an identifier; the server checks the session store for login state.
sessionCookie.extra: The session store holds login state; the cookie carries its identifier. HttpOnly prevents page scripts from reading the cookie, Secure limits transmission to HTTPS, and SameSite mitigates some cross-site request forgery scenarios.
sessionCookie.footer: This illustrates a common browser session cookie flow; behavior depends on the application.

accessSecretToken.lead: After authentication, a client may receive an access token for API calls and a longer-lived secret token for obtaining a new access token. In OAuth, the latter is usually called a refresh token.
accessSecretToken.overview:
flowchart LR
 C[Client] -->|Login credentials| A[Authentication server]
 A -->|Access and refresh tokens| C
 C -->|Access token| B[Business server]
 B -->|Response| C
 C -.->|Refresh token when needed| A
accessSecretToken.overviewNote: The secret token in this example is a refresh token. Issuance and rotation depend on the system design.
accessSecretToken.extra: An access token is sent to the resource server, often in Authorization: Bearer. A refresh token is sent to the authentication server. A client secret identifies a confidential application and is a different credential.
accessSecretToken.footer: This is a general token login flow. Actual issuance, validation, and revocation depend on the system.

sso.lead: Single sign-on (SSO) lets an application delegate authentication to an external identity provider. The user authenticates through browser redirects, and the application creates its own session. Signing out of the application and the identity provider are separate operations. This example uses OpenID Connect (OIDC) authorization code flow with a server-side application.
sso.overview:
flowchart LR
 U[User] -->|Acts| B[Browser]
 B -->|Access and callback| A[Application]
 B -->|Authentication and optional logout| I[Identity provider]
 A -->|Exchange authorization code| I
 I -.->|Optional logout notification| A
sso.overviewNote: The browser follows redirects; the application and identity provider maintain separate sessions. The dashed line represents an optional notification when both sides support and configure it.
sso.supplement:
Sessions and logout scope

SessionPurposeEffect of logout
Application sessionIdentifies the user on later application requests.Ending it signs the user out of this application; the provider session may remain active.
Identity provider sessionRemembers authentication so other applications can reuse it.Ending it usually requires authentication again; existing application sessions do not necessarily end at the same time.

After local logout, an active provider session may allow the user to sign in again without entering credentials.

Integration and logout boundaries

  • Establish trust: Register the client and exact callback addresses, obtain endpoints and signing keys from trusted configuration, and use HTTPS throughout.
  • Protect the callback: Validate state, bind the authorization code with PKCE, and validate nonce when sent. Validate the ID token signature, issuer, audience, expiry and other applicable claims before creating a session.
  • Map accounts: Identify an external identity by its trusted issuer iss and subject sub. Account creation and linking are application policy; do not link solely on an unverified email address.
  • Logout propagation: Provider logout and notification of other applications are independent capabilities. Front-channel or back-channel notifications require support and configuration and can fail.
  • Token lifetime: Ending sessions does not necessarily revoke issued access tokens. Revoke tokens when needed and supported, and control their lifetimes.

References: OIDC Core · RP-initiated logout · Back-channel logout
sso.footer: This example uses a server-side OIDC application; provider capabilities and parameters vary. See OIDC login, OAuth 2.0 and PKCE, and Session cookie login.

emailCode.lead: A user submits an email address and receives a one-time code. The server verifies the code and establishes a login session; possession of the code demonstrates current access to the mailbox.
emailCode.overview:
flowchart LR
 U[User] -->|Email and code| B[Browser or app]
 B -->|HTTPS requests| A[Authentication service]
 A -->|Store and verify code| R[(Code store)]
 A -->|Send email| M[Email provider]
 M -->|Deliver code| E[Mailbox]
 E -->|User reads code| U
 A -->|Create session| S[(Session store)]
 A -->|Session cookie| B
emailCode.overviewNote: The code is used for this authentication attempt; a new session maintains subsequent login state.
emailCode.extra: Use cryptographically secure random codes, short expirations, one-time consumption, and rate limits. Protect stored verification values, avoid account enumeration, and use HTTPS. Email codes depend on mailbox security and are not phishing-resistant multifactor authentication.
emailCode.footer: This example uses a session cookie; other systems may issue tokens.

threeDSecure.lead: 3D Secure (3DS) lets a merchant request cardholder authentication through the card network and issuing bank. The issuer assesses risk and may require a challenge. Payment authorization is a separate step.
threeDSecure.overview:
flowchart LR
 U[Cardholder] -->|Submit payment| M[Merchant or payment provider]
 M -->|3DS request| D[Directory server]
 D -->|Authentication request| A[Issuer authentication system]
 A -.->|Challenge when needed| U
 A -->|Authentication result| D
 D -->|Authentication result| M
 M -->|Payment authorization| P[Payment network]
 P -->|Authorization request| I[Issuer]
threeDSecure.overviewNote: The three domains are the acquirer, interoperability, and issuer domains. Deployments and roles vary.
threeDSecure.extra: Frictionless and challenge are possible authentication paths, not guarantees of success. Liability shift depends on network rules and transaction outcomes. 3DS does not prevent a user from being tricked into approving a fraudulent transaction.
threeDSecure.footer: This is a common 3DS flow; follow the applicable payment provider and card network requirements.

awsSts.lead: AWS Security Token Service (STS) issues temporary credentials for an IAM role. This example uses cross-account AssumeRole: permission to assume a role and permission to access a resource are separate checks.
awsSts.overview:
flowchart LR
 C[Caller] -->|AssumeRole| S[STS]
 S -->|Check trust and permissions| I[IAM policies]
 S -->|Temporary credentials| C
 C -->|Signed request and session token| R[AWS resource service]
 R -->|Authorized response| C
awsSts.overviewNote: This example uses a cross-account role; federation and AWS service credential paths differ.
awsSts.extra: Session policies can restrict role permissions but do not expand the role’s identity-based permissions. AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity and AssumeRoleWithSAML use different federation inputs. Explicit denies and other applicable policy limits still apply.
awsSts.footer: This example covers programmatic cross-account AssumeRole; other STS operations have different requirements.

awsIam.lead: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) helps control who can perform actions on AWS resources. This example follows a role session reading an Amazon S3 object in the same account.
awsIam.overview:
flowchart LR
 C[Caller] -->|Signed read request| S[S3 service]
 S -->|Authenticate and evaluate| P[IAM authorization]
 P -->|Allow or deny| S
 S -->|Read if allowed| R[(S3 object)]
 S -->|Result or error| C
awsIam.overviewNote: The caller already has temporary role credentials. IAM authorization here represents AWS evaluation, not a public IAM API call for every request.
awsIam.extra: Identity and resource policies can grant permissions. Permissions boundaries, session policies, and applicable organization policies can limit access; direct resource-policy grants to certain principals have special rules. Cross-account access generally requires permission on both sides. A role trust policy governs assumption of the role, while resource access is evaluated separately.
awsIam.footer: This is a simplified same-account request. See AWS STS for obtaining role credentials and AWS policy evaluation for details.
